dkim_key_too_short.why: Keys under 1024 bits can be factored at modest cost: 512-bit keys have been broken in hours for about a hundred dollars of cloud computing. Whoever does so can sign mail that passes as yours with receivers that still accept such keys. RFC 8301 forbids verifiers from accepting them, so major providers already treat your signatures as invalid, which hurts your deliverability too.
dkim_key_too_short.fix:
1. Generate a new 2048-bit DKIM key in your mail provider's settings (under a new selector if possible) and publish its TXT record.
2. Switch signing to the new key.
3. Revoke the old key now: set the "{selector}" record to `v=DKIM1; p=` (empty key) so nobody can use it, then remove it later. Run the scan again.

cookie_depth.name: Cookie scope
cookie_depth.description: Looks past the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite flags: whether cookies with the __Host- and __Secure- prefixes follow the rules browsers enforce, and whether session cookies are shared with every subdomain.

cookie_prefix_invalid.title: Browsers refuse your cookie "{cookie_name}"
cookie_prefix_invalid.summary: The cookie "{cookie_name}" uses the __Host- or __Secure- prefix but breaks its rules, so browsers silently refuse to store it.
cookie_prefix_invalid.why: The __Secure- prefix promises that a cookie always has the Secure attribute; __Host- also promises Path=/ and no Domain attribute, so the cookie is locked to exactly your host. Browsers enforce these promises by dropping any prefixed cookie that breaks them. The protection you meant to get is therefore missing, and if this is your login or session cookie, users may be logged out or unable to log in at all.
cookie_prefix_invalid.fix:
1. Find where your application sets "{cookie_name}" (framework session settings or a `Set-Cookie` header).
2. For a __Host- cookie set `Secure` and `Path=/`, and remove any `Domain=` attribute. For a __Secure- cookie set `Secure`.
3. Serve the site over HTTPS only, since Secure cookies require it.
4. Run the scan again.

cookie_domain_too_broad.title: Your session cookie "{cookie_name}" is shared with every subdomain of {domain}
cookie_domain_too_broad.summary: The session cookie "{cookie_name}" is set with Domain={domain}, so browsers send it to {domain} and to every subdomain under it.
cookie_domain_too_broad.why: Without a Domain attribute a cookie goes back only to the host that set it. With Domain={domain}, every subdomain receives your users' session cookie: a forgotten staging server, a marketing site run by a third party, a subdomain taken over through a dangling DNS record, or a page with user content. Any of them can read the cookie and impersonate your users. The attack needs control of one subdomain, so the risk is low but real.
cookie_domain_too_broad.fix:
1. Remove the `Domain=` attribute from the "{cookie_name}" cookie (in most frameworks, leave the session cookie domain setting empty). The cookie then stays host-only.
2. Better still, rename it with the `__Host-` prefix (`__Host-session; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`), which browsers lock to your exact host.
3. If several subdomains really need one login, use a dedicated authentication host and short-lived tokens instead of a shared cookie.
4. Run the scan again.

exposed_files.name: Forgotten files
exposed_files.description: Looks for files that should never be public but often are: database dumps, backup copies of source code, site archives, macOS .DS_Store files, source maps with your original code, and a web server's default page. Each hit is confirmed by the file's content.

database_dump_exposed.title: A database dump with data can be downloaded at {path}
database_dump_exposed.summary: Anyone can download {path}, an SQL dump of your database that contains data rows, not just the table structure.
database_dump_exposed.why: A database dump is a full copy of your data: customer records, e-mail addresses, password hashes, orders. Automated scanners request paths like {path} on every site all day, so assume it has already been downloaded. Depending on what the tables hold, this can be a personal-data breach you must report (for example under GDPR or KVKK).
database_dump_exposed.fix:
1. Delete {path} from the web server now (and any other dump files next to it).
2. Keep backups outside the web root, or in private storage that is never served over HTTP.
3. Check your server's access logs for downloads of this file and treat its contents as exposed: rotate the database passwords and API keys stored in it, and assess whether personal data must be reported.
4. Run the scan again.

source_backup_exposed.title: A backup of your PHP source code can be read at {path}
source_backup_exposed.summary: {path} returns PHP source code as plain text instead of running it, so anyone can read it.
source_backup_exposed.why: Editors and deployment tools leave copies such as .bak, ~ or .save next to the real file. The web server does not run them as PHP; it hands them out as text. Configuration files like wp-config.php hold the database password and secret keys, which an attacker can use directly. Other source files reveal how your application works and where it is weak.
source_backup_exposed.fix:
1. Delete {path} and any other backup copies (*.bak, *~, *.save, *.old, *.swp) from the web root.
2. If the file held passwords or keys (for wp-config.php: database password, authentication keys and salts), change all of them now.
3. Block such files in the server configuration, for example in nginx: `location ~* (\.bak|\.old|\.save|\.swp|~)$ { deny all; }`.
4. Run the scan again.

archive_backup_exposed.title: A site archive can be downloaded at {path}
archive_backup_exposed.summary: Anyone can download {path}, a compressed archive at a typical backup location.
archive_backup_exposed.why: Archives like this are usually a full copy of the website: source code, configuration files with passwords, and sometimes uploaded files and database dumps. GuardHub confirms that the file is an archive by its first bytes; it does not open or keep it. Attackers' scanners request these names on every site.
archive_backup_exposed.fix:
1. Delete {path} from the web server now.
2. Store backups outside the web root or in private storage.
3. Assume the archive was downloaded: change the passwords and keys it may contain (database, mail, API keys) and check your access logs.
4. Run the scan again.

ds_store_exposed.title: A macOS .DS_Store file is public at {path}
ds_store_exposed.summary: {path} is a .DS_Store file left behind by macOS Finder. It lists the names of the files in that folder.
ds_store_exposed.why: When a folder is uploaded from a Mac, Finder's hidden .DS_Store file often goes with it. It contains the names of the files and folders that were there, including ones that are not linked anywhere, such as backups, old admin pages or private documents. Attackers use these names to find files to download. On its own it reveals names, not contents.
ds_store_exposed.fix:
1. Delete .DS_Store files from the server (`find /var/www -name .DS_Store -delete`).
2. Exclude them from deployments (add `.DS_Store` to .gitignore and to your upload or rsync exclude list).
3. Optionally block them in the server, for example in nginx: `location ~ /\.DS_Store { deny all; }`.
4. Run the scan again.

source_map_exposed.title: Your JavaScript source map exposes the original code of {source_count} file(s)
source_map_exposed.summary: The source map {path} is public and contains the original, unminified source code of {source_count} file(s).
source_map_exposed.why: Source maps help developers debug minified JavaScript. When they include the original code (sourcesContent), anyone can read your front-end code with its comments, internal API routes, feature flags and sometimes keys that were never meant to be shipped. This is not a vulnerability by itself, but it makes finding one much easier.
source_map_exposed.fix:
1. Stop publishing source maps in production builds (for example Vite: `build.sourcemap: false`; webpack: `devtool: false`; Next.js: `productionBrowserSourceMaps: false`, the default).
2. If you need them for error tracking, upload them to your error tracker (for example Sentry) instead of serving them, or build them without sourcesContent.
3. Remove the .map files from the server and run the scan again.

default_page_exposed.title: Your home page is {server}'s default welcome page
default_page_exposed.summary: The address you scanned shows the stock welcome page of {server}, not your site.
default_page_exposed.why: A default page usually means the web server is not configured for this name: the real site is on another address, or the server was set up and forgotten. It tells visitors and attackers which software you run and that the server may not be maintained. This is advice, not a vulnerability.
default_page_exposed.fix:
1. If this address should serve your site, add a server block or virtual host for this name pointing to your application.
2. If it should not serve anything, make the default server return an error or redirect, for example in nginx: `server { listen 80 default_server; return 444; }`.
3. Remove the default index page from the web root and run the scan again.

js_libraries.name: Outdated JavaScript libraries
js_libraries.description: Finds well-known JavaScript libraries your home page loads (jQuery, jQuery UI, Bootstrap, AngularJS, Moment, Handlebars, DOMPurify, Vue and others) and checks the exact version against public vulnerability advisories (OSV). A library is reported only when its version is certain: read from the library's own header inside the file, or from a public CDN address that contains the version.

vulnerable_js_library.title: {library} {version} on your site has known vulnerabilities
vulnerable_js_library.summary: Your home page loads {library} {version} ({script}). Public advisories list vulnerabilities in this version: {advisories}.
vulnerable_js_library.why: Every visitor's browser runs this library. The listed advisories describe how attackers can abuse it, most often cross-site scripting (running their own code in your visitors' browsers) when your pages pass untrusted input to the affected functions. GuardHub cannot see from outside whether your code uses those functions, so this is rated medium: the risk is real, but it depends on how the library is used. Attackers' tools look for exactly these version numbers.
vulnerable_js_library.fix:
1. Upgrade {library} to its latest release. The lowest version that fixes every listed advisory is {fixed_version} (a dash means no fixed release exists yet: replace the library or stop using the affected feature).
2. Major upgrades can change behaviour (for example jQuery 1.x/2.x to 3.x): test your pages, and use the library's migration guide or plugin while you update your code.
3. If you load it from a CDN, change the version in the script address; if you serve it yourself, replace the file and clear caches.
4. Run the scan again.

content_signals.name: Page content loading
content_signals.description: Reads your home page's HTML the way a browser does and checks what it loads: scripts, stylesheets, frames, images and media over insecure http:// on an HTTPS page (mixed content), and scripts from other sites without Subresource Integrity.

mixed_content_active.title: Your HTTPS page loads scripts, styles or frames over insecure http://
mixed_content_active.summary: {count} script, stylesheet or frame address(es) on your home page use http://, for example {example}.
mixed_content_active.why: Browsers block these requests on an HTTPS page ("mixed content"), so the parts of your page that depend on them break for every visitor. Where they do load, for example in older browsers, anyone on the network path (public Wi-Fi, a compromised router) can replace the file and take over the page: read what visitors type, change what they see.
mixed_content_active.fix:
1. Change each address to https:// (for example {example}). Most CDNs and services support it; if a host does not, serve the file from your own site.
2. Prefer relative or https:// addresses in templates and content, and fix any hard-coded http:// links in your CMS settings.
3. As a safety net, the header `Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests` makes browsers request https:// instead.
4. Run the scan again.

mixed_content_passive.title: Your HTTPS page loads images or media over insecure http://
mixed_content_passive.summary: {count} image, audio or video address(es) on your home page use http://, for example {example}.
mixed_content_passive.why: Current browsers try the https:// address instead or show a "not fully secure" warning; if the file is not available over https, it is missing. Older browsers load it in clear, so anyone on the network path can see what visitors look at and replace the images.
mixed_content_passive.fix:
1. Change each address to https:// (for example {example}), or serve the files from your own site.
2. Fix hard-coded http:// addresses in your templates, CMS content and settings.
3. Optionally add `Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests`.
4. Run the scan again.

sri_missing.title: Scripts from other sites run without an integrity check
sri_missing.summary: {count} script(s) from other sites are loaded without an integrity attribute, for example {example}.
sri_missing.why: These scripts run with full access to your page. If the other site or CDN is ever compromised, or the file is changed, the new code runs for all your visitors. Subresource Integrity (an integrity="sha384-..." attribute) makes the browser refuse a file that no longer matches. It only works for files that never change, such as a library at a fixed version; analytics and chat widgets that change all the time cannot use it. This is a best practice, not a weakness on its own.
sri_missing.fix:
1. For fixed-version files (libraries from a CDN), add the integrity and crossorigin attributes; CDNs such as cdnjs and jsDelivr show the exact tag to copy.
2. Alternatively, serve the file from your own site.
3. For scripts that change on their own (analytics, chat, tag managers), choose providers you trust and limit them with a Content-Security-Policy.
4. Run the scan again.
